contentSections.body: Pick something you actually use, or would genuinely use, AI assistance for more than once a month — not a hypothetical. A recurring email type, a regular data or content task, a weekly planning or admin routine. Something with real stakes, even modest ones, and a real, repeatable shape.

contentSections.title: A written routine with the time it costs and what it catches
contentSections.brief: You have a real, recurring AI-assisted task. Build a written verification routine for it: name the task's actual stakes, identify its specific failure modes (not generic 'errors'), attach a concrete check to each failure mode, bound the total time, and state the escalation rule for when a check fails. Then test the routine against one real or realistic instance of the task and report honestly on what it actually caught, missed, or cost.
contentSections.deliverable: A written routine (stakes assessment, named failure modes, a check for each, a time budget, an escalation rule) plus a record of running it once on a real instance of the task — what it found, what it took, and one honest note on a weakness in the routine itself.

stages.title: Assess stakes and name failure modes
stages.instructions: State the task plainly, then assess its real stakes using irreversibility, who's affected, and reach. Then list the 2-4 specific ways this exact task tends to go wrong — not 'it might have errors,' but the actual failure modes you've seen or can reasonably predict for this specific kind of work.
stages.checkpoint: You have a one-paragraph stakes assessment and a short list of specific, named failure modes for this exact task.

stages.title: Attach checks, bound the time, set the escalation rule
stages.instructions: For each failure mode, write the specific check that would catch it — naming what you'd actually look at and against what source, using the ideas from this module (targeted spot-checks, independent sources, well-set-up second-model checks where appropriate). Add a total time budget you could realistically hold to on a busy week, and a clear rule for what happens if a check turns something up.
stages.checkpoint: Every named failure mode has a specific attached check, the routine has a stated time budget, and there's an explicit escalation rule.

stages.title: Run it once and report honestly
stages.instructions: Apply the routine to one real or realistic instance of the task. Note how long it actually took versus your budget, what it found (even if 'nothing wrong this time'), and — the most useful part — one honest weakness in the routine itself: a failure mode it doesn't cover, or a check that turned out weaker in practice than it looked on paper.
stages.checkpoint: You have a run record with actual time taken, actual findings, and one named weakness in the routine as written.

rubric.criterion: The task is genuinely recurring and the stakes assessment is specific to it
rubric.meets: The stakes assessment names concrete reasons (who's affected, how reversible, how far it reaches) rather than a generic 'this matters.'

rubric.criterion: Failure modes are specific to this exact task
rubric.meets: Each named failure mode describes a particular way THIS task breaks, not a generic category like 'inaccuracy.'

rubric.criterion: Each check is genuinely targeted and, where relevant, genuinely independent
rubric.meets: Checks name a specific source or sampling approach with real power to catch the named failure — not a vague 'review carefully.'

rubric.criterion: The routine is bounded and realistically repeatable
rubric.meets: A stated time budget that could plausibly survive a busy or low-capacity week, not an open-ended 'be thorough.'

rubric.criterion: The report is honest about what the routine actually did
rubric.meets: The run record names a real weakness or gap, not just a success story — an honest routine improves; a flattering one doesn't.

contentSections.body: A routine that survives being used is worth more than a thorough one that only gets followed in week one — the honest report on its weakness is what makes it improvable.

title: Checkpoint — Verifying Efficiently
description: Ten questions: six from this module, four reaching back to Fabrication — the only earlier module in this phase so far. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve stakes-sizing, targeted spot-checking, source independence, and routine-building without looking them up

contentSections.title: What stuck
Checkpoint — Verifying Efficiently
contentSections.framing: This is only the second module in the phase, so the pulls lean heavily on this module, with a real slice reaching back to Fabrication rather than a full 4/4/2 split — there isn't a third module yet to pull from.

questions.from: This module — What are you actually risking if this is wrong
questions.prompt: What should actually determine how much verification effort a task gets?

options.label: What being wrong would actually cost — irreversibility, who's affected, and how far the answer reaches
How confident the AI's tone sounded
How long the AI's answer was

questions.explanation: Tone and length carry no information about real-world stakes — the three legitimate factors are irreversibility, who's affected, and reach.

questions.from: This module — Spot-checking that finds errors rather than reassures
questions.prompt: Why is checking only the first few items of a long repetitive AI output a weak spot-check?

options.label: The start is the part most tightly anchored to the prompt and least likely to show drift or edge-case failure
The first items are always randomly selected by the model
It's actually a strong check, not a weak one

questions.explanation: Drift and edge-case failure tend to show up later or in atypical items — sampling only the start mostly confirms the easiest part worked.

questions.from: This module — Checking against a source rather than against your memory
questions.prompt: Why doesn't your memory agreeing with an AI's claim strongly confirm the claim is accurate?

options.label: Your memory and the model may share the same popular source of error, so agreement can just mean shared exposure, not accuracy
Human memory is always less reliable than AI output
It does strongly confirm accuracy — agreement is the best evidence available

questions.explanation: Verification strength requires genuine independence between the check and the claim — a memory drawn from the same popular sources as the model's training data isn't independent.

questions.from: This module — Asking a second model, and when that's circular
questions.prompt: What makes 'are you sure?' asked in the same conversation a weak verification step?

options.label: It's answered by the same process with no new access to any external source — a claim checked against itself
Models are programmed to always say yes to that specific question
It's actually a strong check when asked twice

questions.explanation: The follow-up is generated the same way the original claim was — a plausible continuation, not a lookup against something new.

questions.from: This module — Building a check routine for work you repeat
questions.prompt: Why does a written, bounded routine beat 'remembering to be careful' for a task done every week?

options.label: It doesn't depend on having full energy or memory to reconstruct the judgment call each time, so it survives a low-capacity week
Written routines are inherently more thorough than any judgment call could be
There's no real difference between the two approaches

questions.explanation: The support-team-lead example showed the same person checking carefully in week one and skimming in week six — nothing about the task changed, only capacity did, which is exactly what a written routine is built to survive.

questions.from: This module — Building a check routine for work you repeat
questions.prompt: What's the risk of a verification routine with no stated escalation rule for a failed check?

options.label: A failed check can get quietly waved through under deadline pressure instead of triggering a real response
There's no risk — routines don't need escalation rules
The routine will automatically stop the task from being sent

questions.explanation: Without a stated rule for what happens on failure, a found problem has no guaranteed consequence — it's easy to notice something's off and ship anyway when rushed.

questions.from: Previous module — Fabrication
questions.prompt: A fabricated case citation is best understood, mechanically, as:

options.label: The model completing a highly regular shape with specifics it isn't actually retrieving from anywhere
A deliberate lie the model tells when asked a leading question
A memory error where a real citation got garbled

questions.explanation: From Fabrication: there's no honesty step or memory-retrieval step being failed — it's the same plausible-shape generation process regardless of whether the citation turns out to be real.

questions.from: Previous module — Fabrication
questions.prompt: Why is decimal precision in an unsourced statistic not evidence it's accurate?

options.label: Precision is a cheap formatting choice a model can apply to an invented number as easily as a real one
Decimal points are strong evidence of a real measurement behind the number
Models cannot generate decimal numbers unless they're accurate

questions.explanation: From Fabrication: a real statistic's precision reflects an actual measurement process; a generated number's precision just reflects a common formatting shape.

questions.from: Previous module — Fabrication
questions.prompt: Which question shape reliably raises fabrication risk, independent of topic?

options.label: A fixed enumeration quota, like 'list six examples,' when fewer genuine ones may exist
Any question about a well-known scientific constant
Any question phrased politely

questions.explanation: From Fabrication: a fixed quota pushes the model to fill every slot whether or not that many genuine examples are well represented, producing invented items past the real ones.

questions.from: Previous module — Fabrication
questions.prompt: Why is believing 'careful prompting means I no longer need to fact-check' considered more dangerous than not knowing any fabrication-reducing technique at all?

options.label: The output now sounds appropriately hedged and reliable, which makes the remaining risk less visible rather than actually gone
Careful prompting measurably increases fabrication
It isn't more dangerous — this is the module's actual recommendation

questions.explanation: From Fabrication: prompting techniques improve the surface appearance of reliability without adding an actual fact-check, so trusting that appearance instead of verifying is a worse position than appropriate default suspicion.
